The Jewish religion is very weak as regards the feelings of religious awe. It is even as if there were no such thing. The Jewish religion is almost entirely rational; it can be comprehended through rational arguments alone. But when one is considering matters of religion one must not only employ arguments; one must also have feelings of religious awe. The Jews have none of these. They do not sense the awe that the majesty of God should inspire in us. The Jewish people lack this important component in our religious lives. This is why we Jews are so weak when it comes to matters of religion, why we have such little inclination towards faith, and why the majority of our people abandon their religion.

The first great religious awakening took place in the 16th century, when the Reformation began in Germany. This religious awakening was very important and very great. But it was not enough. The religious awakening that took place among the Jews was insufficient. Only when it occurred among Christians, it was good. And if it does not occur among Christians, this is no misfortune, for the Jewish religion has not produced any results among us.

We Jews have not had this sense of religious awe since time immemorial. This sense of religious awe is necessary in order to appreciate God. And there is no appreciation of God among the Jews. This is a weakness of Judaism. God's greatness is hidden from us, because the world around us makes us think that the world is too great for the majesty of God, that the majesty of God is not great enough. And because God's greatness is hidden from us, our religion is not great either, it is not the religion of the Jewish people.</s>

What can we learn from the phenomenon of fear?

In terms of fear, we find two opposing approaches. We can be afraid of fear itself. This is how we react to the situation in which we have to make a difficult decision, such as whether to accept the post of governor of a province. We are afraid of possible reactions of the provincial inhabitants; in the final analysis, our fear is the reaction to a potential fear of others. When we fear fear, we do so with a certain degree of certainty. We know we will be afraid, which gives us the opportunity to take certain preventive measures: to prepare, for instance, a speech we will present in the event of an outbreak of unrest. We can also avoid such situations altogether, but this is always a lesser alternative.

However, the opposite approach can also be observed. It is based on the notion of a fear of fearlessness. This is the fear of the void and of the uncertainty associated with it. This is the fear that occurs when we are forced to make a decision in which all potential consequences are unknown to us. We are afraid of the prospect that we will not be afraid and will find ourselves paralyzed in the face of the unknown. The fear that the decision may turn out to be the wrong one, the fear of making the right choice, and the fear of failure all derive from the same source.

Both approaches are equally rational. They are both grounded in the rational fear of the unknown. We are afraid of fear because we fear uncertainty. This is the source of all fear.

How can we conquer fear? In our attempt to find an answer to this question, we may ask another question first: what is the ultimate source of fear? Our own existence may not be the only cause of fear. Our existence may be a mere consequence of fear. The fear of our own existence is the fear of the void. This is the fear of death. Death is the ultimate source of fear. We can conquer fear only by conquering death.

How can we conquer death? The solution to this question can be found in the words of the ancient Greek poet and philosopher Plato, who wrote: "He who is truly wise shall fear death as the most fearful of all events."1

In order to understand the words of Plato, we must first understand the meaning of the word "fearful." Fear is an emotion that arises in a situation where we do not know what will happen to us in the future. In other words, we cannot see the future and are unable to predict it. The future may bring death, the greatest fear. Therefore, in order to be truly wise, we must have an unshakable faith in the existence of the future, a faith in the existence of a future that is not dependent on death.

We can conquer death by faith. We can conquer fear by believing in the possibility of overcoming the ultimate fear. If we believe in such a possibility, then we can be truly wise.

Is there a greater cause of fear than death?
